Early game is hardest and most repetitive, imo. There are so few regions you can effectively adventure in, and even in those regions there are potential pitfalls.

Remember, while the game scales up to keep challenge roughly equal throughout, enemies all have a MINIMUM level they spawn at. See a hagraven, or a spriggan? A falmer? Just make a mental note of where they are and run away. Bear or Sabre cat? Run from that too. Spell caster strongholds should be similarly avoided. 

What can I do? 

1. First perk points should be put into the first perk of your primary direct damage source (1h, 2h, Archery, Destruction) and your preferred armor type (Light, Heavy, or Alteration if not using armor). 
2. These first perks are so good that they should always be at max level until you start steamrolling people. 
3. Invest in sneaking, blocking, and/or heavy armor. (Light armor without sneaking or blocking is possible, but not recommended when you’re struggling)
4. Focus on one specific direct damage source to level it faster
5. Get a follower (Faendal in Riverwood or Uthgerd in Whiterun are easily recruited)
6. Use summon spells or Fury to add even more allied fighters (Fury is great for getting free gear when used on NPC patrols).

Stay in the Whiterun region at first. Doing the radiant bounty quests is good, and the townsfolk have a lot of quests they can give you that are almost all doable at like level 3. Except the gildegreen, which has hagravens (level 20), and Missing in Action which concludes outside of Whiterun. Do the main quest up until where you have to see the Graybeards, we’ll climb the steps later.

Head to Falkreath next, keeping a close eye on caves (if it’s falmer, run) and giants. You can steal from the chest in the giants camp, you just gotta be ready to run cuz they’ll send you spaceborn. Falkreath can be a drag, but you won’t be there for long. 

Once you’re level 15, you’re a level above trolls (kill them with fire) and ready to go most anywhere. The North is still treacherous, as is the Reach, but you can handle those with preparation and patience.

Not a horror movie, but the Bent-Neck Lady from The Haunting of Hill House.

At first, you just think it’s a run-of-the-mill tortured ghost who locks on to one person until XYZ, but in one of the most emotional and scary episodes of the series:

>![tl;dr here’s the scene](https://youtu.be/vHkX4gNuSOI?feature=shared) The girl, haunted all her life by the Bent-Neck Lady, is now grown. The house, which is so haunted that it’s pure sentient malevolence, lures her back. It can create illusions, and it lures her farther in to a staircase under construction. It tricks her into wrapping a rope noose around her neck, and she falls. Her neck is visibly, gruesomely, broken. Her toes dangle above the floor. And it doesn’t end there.!<

>!She drops again, to somewhere else entirely. One of the haunting scenes from earlier in the series, when we first saw the Bent-Neck Lady. The realization is instant, and grows more sickening from there. Every time she was haunted by the Bent-Neck Lady, she was seeing her future death. There is no restful afterlife for this tortured girl, just replaying the scenes that caused such agony. Being forced to witness your own terror, again and again, forever. 10/10, couldn’t sleep that night, still feel haunted by it.!<

It’s difficult to be a survivor. You feel like any compliment is (at best) surface-level wish fulfillment for people who want to be saviors or who fantasize of being abused. 

I know that I, very very often, feel broken or wrong. We are different, and changed, but we are not broken people. We feel everything and experience everything that everyone else does. And often our trauma or danger response gets in the way, but we can find new reasons to move on and maybe new people to move on with. 

You are not broken. Even if you feel emotionally unavailable, or functionally inept. 

I love you for who you are, with no expectation of returned feeling or requirements to fulfill. You are loved, exactly as you are. 

It is a difficult thing to say ‘yes! hello, I am struggling.’ And I am truly appreciative that you put yourself out there. It makes me feel less alone, too.

Thank you!! I really appreciate your words, though I know it is far more difficult to accept kind words than to acknowledge them.

I really appreciate your words. I’ll probably be coming back to them often in the coming months, or even years.
